name: Inversions After Shuffle
description: You are given a permutation of integers from 1 to n . Exactly once you apply the following operation to this permutation: pick a random segment and shuffle its elements. Formally: Pick a random segment (continuous subsequence) from l to r . All segments are equiprobable. Let k = r - l + 1 , i.e. the length of the chosen segment. Pick a random permutation of integers from 1 to k , p 1 , p 2 , ..., p k . All k ! permutation are equiprobable. This permutation is applied to elements of the chosen segment, i.e. permutation a 1 , a 2 , ..., a l - 1 , a l , a l + 1 , ..., a r - 1 , a r , a r + 1 , ..., a n is transformed to a 1 , a 2 , ..., a l - 1 , a l - 1 + p 1 , a l - 1 + p 2 , ..., a l - 1 + p k - 1 , a l - 1 + p k , a r + 1 , ..., a n . Inversion if a pair of elements (not necessary neighbouring) with the wrong relative order. In other words, the number of inversion is equal to the number of pairs ( i , j ) such that i < j and a i > a j . Find the expected number of inversions after we apply exactly one operation mentioned above.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 000 ) — the length of the permutation. The second line contains n distinct integers from 1 to n — elements of the permutation.
output_specification: Print one real value — the expected number of inversions. Your answer will be considered correct if its absolute or relative error does not exceed 10 - 9 . Namely: let's assume that your answer is a , and the answer of the jury is b . The checker program will consider your answer correct, if .
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 749E — Inversions After Shuffle [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
